highlights: Inspection drone integrates visual and thermal data with Percepto AIM
Datasheet lists 24 MP RGB plus thermal imaging for the standard Air Max configuration
Separate OGI payload option supports gas-imaging applications
Percepto Base provides the accompanying docking infrastructure; drone and base ratings are separate

The April 2022 Air datasheet and November 2021 brochure separate Air Max aircraft values—9.5 kg, 157 cm propeller-tip diagonal and IP55—from its 350 kg, 166 × 162 × 168 cm, IP56 base. Aircraft battery/payload mass inclusion is unspecified; diagonal span is not an outer packing box.

Standard Air Max imagery is documented as 24 MP RGB plus thermal. The OGI configuration is separately described, and the dedicated Air Max OGI sheet gives 10.7 kg and a 16 MP RGB plus Ventus gas camera; these are not interchangeable universal standard-aircraft values.

The November 17, 2021 announcement calls Air Max the next generation of Sparrow; a January 2022 supplier account calls it Sparrow’s newest configuration. This establishes a documented succession relationship, not identical hardware across all generations or an alias for current Ranger.

AIM manages autonomous missions and shares geotagged observations. The brochures’ 24/7 cycle depends on returning to a charging/shelter base; it is not a measured continuous flight duration, per-charge battery life or exact charge time. Exact present supply and purchase price remain unverified.

Whole-aircraft IP55 is not borrowed from the standard Air Max/Mobile sheet because this dedicated OGI sheet does not state it.

Percepto AIM supplies remote data management, trend/anomaly reporting and shared geotagged findings. Current Ranger OGI naming and redirected old URLs do not establish identical hardware; historical Air Max OGI remains separate without inherited current specifications or guaranteed stock.

highlights: Autonomous inspection drone with 61 MP full-frame RGB and radiometric thermal cameras
Onboard perception supports repeatable inspection data capture and obstacle avoidance
Harbor docking infrastructure and AIM software support remote operation

The dedicated Ranger page says 61 MP full-frame RGB and radiometric thermal; the current drone-portfolio page says 1 MP full-frame RGB with Boson thermal. The source-text discrepancy remains explicit, without silently correcting a presumed typo or asserting one universal inspected camera configuration.

Percepto Core onboard AI recognizes assets, avoids obstacles and automates inspection maneuvers. AIM provides remote mission orchestration and the page describes up to 30 drones from one interface; fleet concurrency is not one-aircraft flight endurance, safe separation proof or standardized task throughput.

Harbor stores, charges and shelters Ranger between missions. Its hurricane-category-5 test claim belongs to the station; generic airborne rain/snow/wind language supplies no numeric aircraft envelope or ingress rating. Always-available operation does not establish a 24-hour battery or nonstop flight.

The October 27, 2026 Axion SaaS announcement and strategy note retain Ranger/Harbor as hardware data sources while opening analysis to supported third-party sensors and archives. They do not rename the drone Axion, establish a new aircraft model, prove current stock or date Ranger’s first launch.

Supplier BVLOS/type-certification and qualifying-site language is retained as attributed positioning, not an independently verified present permission for every aircraft/operator/site. Selected pages supply no exact complete-aircraft mass, dimensions, numeric endurance, charge time or retail quote; older Air Max figures are not substituted.

highlights: Autonomous optical-gas-imaging platform for industrial emissions inspections
Onboard processing flags possible emissions and supports repeatable data collection
AIM remote operations and Harbor docking infrastructure support inspection workflows

Current Ranger OGI text describes onboard AI emission flagging, automated data collection and remote AIM missions. The portfolio identifies Ventus OGI plus RGB cameras. AI Emission Detector is an analysis feature, not an additional aircraft model or an extra numeric cargo rating.

The June 16, 2025 detector release reports 100 g/h at 90% confidence; the October 1, 2025 supplier method announcement describes 100 g/h at 90% reliability in its test context and 300 g/h in a higher-wind Permian deployment. Conditions and wording remain distinct: these are not universal gas sensitivity, positional accuracy, aircraft speed or inspections-per-hour ratings.

The October 2025 release is a supplier account of EPA Alternative Test Method acceptance under named subparts. Older linked pending-approval wording and a historical camera-only sheet do not establish current blanket compliance. No independent regulator decision or universal site/operator eligibility is verified in this selected aircraft review.

Harbor’s shelter charging, hurricane test and AIM’s up-to-30-drone orchestration describe station/service/fleet roles. They do not establish Ranger OGI mass, ingress protection, continuous airborne duration or full charge time. Air Max OGI’s 10.7 kg, 157 cm and 16 MP figures are not transferred to this current platform.

The October 27, 2026 company strategy explicitly keeps Ranger/Harbor hardware while launching Axion software for supported third-party data as well. Axion’s AI model count and training-data hours are software-development claims, not additional drones or proven per-mission detection accuracy.
